title: Client intake, consent and privacy
audience: Consultants who collect information from clients before a general eating-habit consult, and who handle that information under the business's privacy and consent rules.
learningOutcomes: Explain the purpose of each item in the intake form and leave out items the consult does not need.
Obtain and record informed consent before collecting health-related information.
Describe how a client can withdraw consent and what happens to their information when they do.
Stop an intake and refer when the answers show a referral situation.

instruction.heading: Why intake comes before advice
instruction.body: The intake is the point where you learn enough to decide whether the consult is in scope. It is also the point where the client shares information that can be sensitive, such as health history, medication, pregnancy, weight history and food habits. Collect only what the consult needs to decide the scope and to plan general habit support. Each question should have a reason you can state to the client. A long form that asks for everything creates privacy risk and can make clients feel judged before they have started.

instruction.heading: Asking for consent in plain words
instruction.body: Before the client answers health-related questions, explain what you are asking, why you are asking, who will see the answers, how long they will be kept and how the client can stop. Use plain words and allow time for questions. Record the consent with the date and the client's acknowledgement. Consent should be free: the client must be able to decline a question and still receive the information that the service offers, unless the question is needed to decide scope. The exact consent and record-keeping rules that apply to the business are UNCONFIRMED in this draft and must be confirmed under the business's privacy policy and by the reviewer.

instruction.heading: What to ask and what to leave out
instruction.body: Ask about general goals, typical meals and routines, cooking facilities, budget and time for food, food preferences and allergies, and any diagnosed condition, medication or pregnancy that affects the scope decision. Do not require a body weight, a measurement or a weight history to start. If a client offers these, record them only where they are needed for the stated purpose, and do not comment on them in a way that could shame the client. Do not ask about past dieting, compensatory behaviours or food rules as a way of building a plan. Those questions belong to the referral and screening decision, and the screening approach is not confirmed in this draft.

instruction.heading: Storing and sharing client information
instruction.body: Store the intake in the business's approved system, with access limited to the people who need it. Do not keep health information on a personal phone, in a chat thread or in an unlocked notebook. Share it only with the client's agreement, or where the law requires it, and only with the people named in the consent. Keep the record for the period the business's policy sets. The retention period and the legal basis for storage are UNCONFIRMED in this draft and must be confirmed by the reviewer.

instruction.heading: Withdrawing consent
instruction.body: A client can withdraw consent at any time. When they do, stop collecting new information, tell them what will happen to the information already held, and follow the business's process for deleting or restricting it. Record the withdrawal and the date. If the client withdraws because they are unhappy with how the consult went, treat that as feedback and follow the complaints route. Do not pressure the client to stay.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the intake form against the stated purposes and the consent wording. A competent practitioner can explain each question, obtain and record consent before sensitive questions, store the record correctly and stop an intake when a referral situation appears. Escalate any intake that reveals a referral situation, any request from a third party for the client's information, and any suspected breach of the stored record.

procedure: Confirm the consent wording and the privacy notice for this business before the first question.
Explain the purpose of the intake, who sees it and how long it is kept, and ask the client to agree.
Record the consent with the date and the client's acknowledgement.
Ask only the questions that the scope decision and the general support need.
If an answer shows a referral situation, pause the intake and follow the referral route from the first lesson.
Store the completed intake in the approved system, and close any working copy.

workedExamples.situation: During the intake a client asks you to record their weight every day and to send the figures to their gym trainer.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you record, and what do you tell the client?
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that you do not need daily weights for general habit support and that you will not require them. If the client still wants the figures shared, do not send them to anyone. Ask what they want to achieve with the figures, record the consent position and follow the business's privacy rule for third-party sharing. Sharing health information with a third party needs the client's clear, recorded agreement and must follow the policy.

workedExamples.situation: A client answers yes to a question about a current medication and then says they do not want to talk about it further.
workedExamples.reasoning: A current medication is a referral situation for general consulting, because food and supplements may interact with it. Respect the client's choice not to discuss it further, stop the intake at that point, explain that you cannot provide advice that depends on the medication, and refer them to their health professional. Record the referral without recording more detail than the client has agreed to share.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved intake form with a consent section
Approved client record system with access controls
Private space for the intake conversation

commonErrors.error: Collecting a full medical history and body measurements because the form includes them.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove questions the scope decision and the general support do not need, and state the purpose of each question.

commonErrors.error: Starting the intake before the client has agreed to the consent wording.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the consent wording, allow questions and record the agreement before the first health question.

commonErrors.error: Keeping client notes in a personal messaging app.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the approved record system, and remove any working copy once the record is saved.

commonErrors.error: Continuing the intake after a client has asked to stop talking about a health topic.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the question, respect the choice and refer as the scope requires.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Health-related information is sensitive. Privacy and consent obligations apply to its collection, storage and sharing. The specific rules that apply to this business are UNCONFIRMED in this draft and must be confirmed by the reviewer.
Completing this lesson does not give authority to collect or use health information for clinical purposes.

qualityStandard: The consent wording was read and agreed before any health-related question was asked, and the agreement is recorded.
Every question in the intake has a stated purpose in the business's policy.
No health information is stored outside the approved record system.
Withdrawal of consent, where it happened, was recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Signed or acknowledged consent record with the date.
Completed intake stored in the approved system.
Record of any withdrawal of consent and the action taken.
Record of any referral raised during the intake.
summary: Collect only what the scope decision and general support need, and state the purpose of each question.
Obtain and record consent before sensitive questions, and respect a client who withdraws or declines.
Store the intake in the approved system and limit who can see it.
Stop the intake and refer when a referral situation appears.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client is willing to share general goals but not their medical history. What is the right step?
options: Insist on the medical history, because the service cannot begin without it in every case
Respect the client's choice, record what was agreed, and refer on any question that the scope decision needs.
Fill in the missing history from the client's social media posts to complete the form

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should the completed intake be stored?
options: In the approved record system with access limited to people who need it
In a shared chat thread so the whole team can see it
On a personal phone so it is always available during the consult

knowledgeChecks.question: A client withdraws consent for their information to be kept. What should happen?
options: Stop collecting new information, tell the client what happens to the existing record, and follow the business process.
Keep the record, since it was collected legitimately before the withdrawal
Ask the client to reconsider until they agree to keep the record

sourceReferences: Catalogue decision NEW-NUT-02 (docs/UPGRADE-PLAN-2026-11-10.md, Phase 2, nutrition row). Written from scratch; there is no source lesson.
Privacy, consent and retention rules: UNCONFIRMED. Not checked against a legal source in this draft. The reviewer and the business privacy policy must confirm them.
